wine.name: Frascati Superiore Vigneto Santa Teresa
wine.classification: DOCG since 2011, when the Superiore was raised above the Frascati DOC
wine.grapes: Malvasia di Candia and Malvasia del Lazio, the Puntinata, together the larger part, with Greco; older vintages also held Trebbiano.
wine.sites: A single vineyard of the house in the Santa Teresa district, on the volcanic hills of Frascati, where the vines grow on pozzolana: deep, sandy and well drained soils of old volcanic ash, rich in potash and poor in nitrogen.
wine.making: The must is fermented cool, at a controlled temperature, in stainless steel, and the wine stays in steel tanks until it is bottled, which keeps the scent of the Malvasia; it sees no wood.
wine.glass: Pale straw with green glints; white peach, ripe pear and acacia blossom over a hint of almond, light to medium in body, with fresh acidity and the gently bitter, almond skin close of Malvasia.
wine.ageing: Made to drink within two or three years of the harvest, while the Malvasia is fresh; a ripe vintage holds a little longer, turning towards honey and almond.
wine.serve: 8 to 10 degrees Celsius; no need to decant; a white wine glass of medium size.

label.means: The single vineyard of the house in the Santa Teresa district, whose grapes alone make the wine.
Frascati's higher rank since 2011: Malvasia di Candia and Malvasia del Lazio at least seven tenths of the blend.

records.table: Fontana Candida's Santa Teresa is a single vineyard Frascati Superiore from the volcanic hills of the Castelli Romani: Malvasia di Candia and Malvasia del Lazio with a little Greco, fermented cool in steel. Pale, fresh and almond scented, it suits fish from the Roman coast.
records.story: Frascati is the white of the Castelli Romani, the volcanic hills just south east of Rome, and its rules ask that Malvasia lead the blend. Fontana Candida takes its name from a hill at Monte Porzio Catone, where its cellars have made wine since 1958, by the house's own account. In 1966 Frascati became a DOC, among the early ones of Italy, and the house says it has spent more than sixty years carrying the wine abroad. Beside the plain white it made a Frascati Superiore from a single vineyard of its own, Santa Teresa, where the vines grow on pozzolana, the deep and sandy ash of the old Alban volcano, and ripen in the long, warm days of a Roman autumn. In 2011 the Superiore and the sweet Cannellino were raised above the DOC to DOCG, each with at least seven tenths Malvasia, and Santa Teresa has carried the higher rank since. Its grapes are Malvasia di Candia and the scented Malvasia del Lazio, with Greco, fermented cool in steel. To a sommelier it is a lesson in what Frascati can be beyond the carafe: a dry white with the scent of its grape and the stamp of its soil.

The plan's note is answered in part: the blend is Malvasia di Candia, Malvasia del Lazio (Puntinata) and Greco on the house's page, with Trebbiano in older vintages (i-Italy for 2004, Vino.com for 2015); no source read gave the vineyard's first vintage, so the record gives none.
Founded 1958 rests on the house's page (Gruppo Italiano Vini) and DoctorWine's producer page; the soils, the pozzolana and the warm autumn are from the house's Santa Teresa and territory pages.

The cool steel fermentation rests on Vino.com's sheet (15 to 16 degrees Celsius, hand picking) and i-Italy (cold fermentation); i-Italy alone gives some twelve hours of skin contact for the Malvasia of the 2004 vintage, which is left out.
The note on the plain Frascati DOC is from the US importer's sheet (Frederick Wildman, 2023 Frascati DOC).

Left out for want of a second source: the ownership history (one account has Brown-Forman selling Fontana Candida with Bolla to Gruppo Italiano Vini in 2008), the Roman villa said to stand under the cellar and to have been Horace's, and the years of the house's export to America.

Decanter (Italy, Roman triumph) calls the house the largest Frascati producer and says Frascati's name had suffered by the 1980s; neither is in the record, the first being a ranking and the second resting on one source.
The plan's why and the region's producers line (carried Frascati abroad) agree with the house's own claim, which the story hedges as the house's account.

wine.name: Donna Adriana, earlier labelled Vigna Adriana
wine.grapes: Viognier, about four fifths, with Malvasia del Lazio, the Puntinata, for the rest, in the vintages sold as Donna Adriana.
wine.sites: The estate's vineyards at Grottaferrata, on the volcanic hills of the Castelli Romani at some 250 to 270 metres, replanted in close rows between 1988 and 1993.
wine.making: Fermented in stainless steel at about 18 degrees Celsius, by the house's account; a small part, about a seventh by the house's sheet, is fermented in barriques, which lends it a light touch of wood.
wine.glass: Apricot, white peach and honeysuckle over a ripe, almost oily texture from the Viognier, lifted by the almond and fresh acidity of the Malvasia; full in body and dry, with a long, gently bitter finish.
wine.ageing: Generous on release, it keeps for a decade and more in a good vintage: the house has poured bottles thirteen years old at its own tastings.
wine.serve: 11 to 13 degrees Celsius, the house's own advice being 12; no need to decant; a generous white wine glass.

label.means: The name the white carries on later labels; early vintages were sold as Vigna Adriana, some labelled Frascati.
The regional rank, which allows a Viognier led blend that Frascati's Malvasia led rules would refuse.

records.table: Castel de Paolis's Donna Adriana, once labelled Vigna Adriana, is the Grottaferrata estate's white of Viognier with Malvasia del Lazio, grown on volcanic soil in the Frascati hills yet sold as Lazio IGT. Broad, dry and apricot scented, it suits a fish course or white meat.
records.story: In 1974 a politician with a love of the vine bought a first small parcel at Grottaferrata, in the Castelli Romani, and in 1977 added the plots beside it, by the house's account. Until 1985 the grapes went to the local co-operatives. That year, then an under secretary in the government, he began a project with a professor of viticulture to trial the native grapes of the hills beside international ones, and between 1988 and 1993 the whole estate was replanted in close rows. Its first wines came in 1993, eight years after the research began: a Frascati, a Frascati Superiore and the white the house calls Donna Adriana. Sold first as Vigna Adriana, its early vintages were labelled Frascati; in later ones Viognier leads, about four fifths, and the wine carries the regional Lazio IGT, since Frascati's rules ask for Malvasia. When the cellar was restored, Roman water cisterns were found beneath part of its floor. To a sommelier the estate is a lesson in how the Castelli Romani changed from the 1980s: research, closer planting and whites that set out to be more than carafe Frascati.

A swap of the wine's name only, house and key kept, is proposed for the checker: the house's own pages name the white Donna Adriana (Viognier about four fifths with Malvasia del Lazio, Lazio IGT, among the three whites of 1993), while Vigna Adriana is the name World of Fine Wine, DiWineTaste (2006) and a tasting of the 2001 vintage give; no source read states the change of name in words, so the record says earlier and later labels and leaves the year of the change out.

The plan's note is answered: the house's history puts the first parcel in 1974, the research with the University of Milan from 1985 (another account says 1985 to 1992), the replanting from 1988 to 1993 and the first wines in 1993; founded is left empty because the house dates its land to 1974 and its wines to 1993.

Living names met, none in the fragment: the founder (a politician, then under secretary for agriculture), the professor of viticulture at Milan, the consultant oenologist until 2003 (on people.json), a later oenologist and the founder's son, for people.json.

The barrel part rests on the house's pages (about fifteen per cent for the 2020 vintage, a small share of wood in its award notice of the 2014 vintage); the 18 degrees Celsius of fermentation and the 12 of service are the house's.

Left out for want of a second source: the wine named for the founder's wife, the Roman villa of the Scribonii Libones and the medieval Castrum Pauli under the estate, and one vintage listed with Sauvignon Blanc in the blend.

The region's producers line (led the revival of quality Frascati from the 1980s, whites built on Malvasia del Lazio) sits uneasily beside a flagship led by Viognier; the record says plainly why it is not a Frascati.

wine.name: Montiano
wine.grapes: Merlot alone, after trials of small lots of the grape in vineyard and cellar, by the house's account.
wine.sites: Vineyards at Montefiascone, on the rim of the crater of Lake Bolsena, and at Castiglione in Teverina, in the Viterbo hills of northern Lazio, on volcanic soils at some 300 metres, by the house's account.
wine.making: Macerated on its skins for some ten to twenty days by vintage, the wine ferments in steel tanks or, in some vintages, in barriques, and goes through its malolactic in barrique. It then ages about a year in new barriques before bottling, by the house's sheets.
wine.glass: Black cherry, plum and blackberry over cocoa, vanilla and sweet tobacco; ripe and full in body, with plush, velvety tannin and a long, warm finish.
wine.ageing: Rich and open young, thanks to its ripe Merlot, it gains savoury depth over a decade and more in a cool cellar.
wine.serve: 16 to 18 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle an hour ahead, an older one gently off its sediment; a Bordeaux glass.

label.means: The name of the Merlot, first made with the 1993 vintage; later labels set it under Tenuta Montiano.
Indicazione Geografica Protetta, the regional rank; earlier vintages read Lazio IGT, the older name of the same rank.
The name the family business trades under in its later years, on labels once marked Falesco.

records.table: Falesco's Montiano is the Merlot that drew notice to the reds of northern Lazio: Merlot alone from volcanic hills near Lake Bolsena, aged about a year in new barriques. Plush and dark, with plum and cocoa, it wants an hour in a decanter and a roast beside it.
records.story: The family were growers at Monterubiaglio, on the border of Umbria and Lazio, and in the 1960s built a first cellar to make wine of their own. In 1979 two brothers of the family founded Falesco at Montefiascone, above Lake Bolsena, to bring back the old grapes of the area. Montefiascone is the home of Est! Est!! Est!!!, the white named, the story goes, for a bishop's servant who chalked his verdict on the doors of inns along the road to Rome, and the house makes one, Poggio dei Gelsi. A journey to Bordeaux in 1988, as the house tells it, turned one of the brothers towards a red of his own. He tried small lots of Merlot in vineyard and cellar, and in 1993 came the first Montiano, Merlot alone, aged in new barriques and sold outside the DOC rules, later under the regional Lazio IGT. In 1999 the house bought the Marciliano estate in the hills south of Orvieto, across the Umbrian border, where it built a new cellar, and from 2016, by its account, the founders' daughters took the lead and the business came to trade as Famiglia Cotarella. To a sommelier Montiano is the red that showed the volcanic north of Lazio could give a ripe Merlot made to keep.

others.note: The second Merlot of the Montiano estate, drawn from several vineyards and labelled Lazio IGP.

others.name: Poggio dei Gelsi
others.note: The house's Est! Est!! Est!!! di Montefiascone, the white of Lake Bolsena it names among the wines of its identity.

traps: Montiano is a Lazio IGT, or IGP on later labels, not an Est! Est!! Est!!! di Montefiascone: that DOC is a white, and Montiano is Merlot alone.
Montiano's vineyards lie in northern Lazio by Lake Bolsena, though the house's later cellar at Marciliano lies across the border in Umbria.

The plan's note is answered: the founding of 1979 at Montefiascone, the first Montiano of 1993 and its Lazio IGT (IGP on later sheets) stand on the house's history and Montiano pages and its sheets, with K&D Wines, Cana Wine Company and Benchmark Wine's listings beside them; one merchant puts the Merlot plantings in the late 1980s, the house in 1990.

Both founders are living and on people.json, and the house's later leaders, the founders' daughters, are living: nobody is named; the family of the 1960s cellar, named on the house's page, is described for want of dates.

Making by the house's sheets: maceration of 20 days (1999), 15 days (2013) and 10 days (2017); fermentation wholly in barrique (2013) or in steel cones (2017); malolactic in barrique and twelve months in new barriques; two merchants give twelve months in new French oak for 1998 and 1999, so French is left out of the record for want of the house's word.
The house's page on the 2016 vintage speaks of a closer selection and of 36 months rather than 24, without saying of what; the record leaves it out.

The handover of 2016 and the name Famiglia Cotarella rest on the house's sustainability report of 2024 and its history page; the year the name changed is not given in words, so the record ties it loosely to the handover.

Poggio dei Gelsi is named on the house's history page; its grapes (Roscetto, Trebbiano and Malvasia, in shares that differ by merchant) and the claim that it was the house's first wine rest on merchants alone and are left out.
The Est! Est!! Est!!! legend is told as the Codex region record tells it; the bishop is not named, since no source read gave his dates.

wine.making: Fermented on its skins in stainless steel for some fifteen days, the wine then ages some six to eight months in small oak barriques, by the house's sheets. As a Superiore Riserva it must age at least twenty months in all, six of them in bottle, before release.
wine.glass: Sour cherry, red plum and violets over black pepper, tobacco and a touch of vanilla from the barrique; medium to full in body, with lively acidity, fine but grippy tannin and the faintly bitter close of Cesanese.
wine.ageing: Approachable once released, after its twenty months, it gains depth over five to ten years in a cool cellar.
wine.serve: 15 to 17 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle an hour ahead; a large red wine glass.

records.table: Casale della Ioria's Torre del Piano is a Cesanese del Piglio Superiore Riserva from one vineyard at Acuto, Cesanese di Affile alone, aged some months in small barriques. Cherry scented, peppery and lively, with the faintly bitter close of Cesanese, it suits lamb or a hearty pasta.
records.story: Casale della Ioria is a family farm in the Ciociaria, the hill country of the province of Frosinone, with its cellar on the road between Anagni and Paliano and its vines around Anagni, Acuto and Piglio, the towns of the Cesanese. The house holds that its land has been farmed since the days of the Roman Empire, and it grows the grapes of its hills by organic means: the red Cesanese and Olivella and the white Passerina. In 1986 the family planted the vineyard at Acuto, some 335 metres up on volcanic soil, that gives Torre del Piano, of Cesanese di Affile alone. The appellation had been a DOC since 1973, and in 2008 Cesanese del Piglio was raised to DOCG, the first in Lazio, three years before Frascati's Superiore and Cannellino. Its rules ask the Superiore Riserva for at least twenty months of ageing, six of them in bottle, and a higher strength than the plain wine. Torre del Piano is the house's Riserva: fermented in steel, then aged some months in small barriques before its rest in bottle, and set beside the house's Superiore, Tenuta della Ioria. To a sommelier it is a way into Lazio's one red DOCG: a perfumed, peppery Cesanese with the faintly bitter close of its grape, from a family of growers rather than a large house.

The plan's note is answered in part: the house's sheets give Torre del Piano's vineyard (Acuto, 335 metres, volcanic soil, planted 1986, Guyot) and its ageing (six to eight months in barrique on the newer sheet, eight on an older one); the Riserva's twenty months, six in bottle, are from the Ministry's copy of the rules and ARSIAL's volume of 2026.

Founded is left empty: 1921 appears in an importer's profile (Tuttilili) and one other secondary account, but not on the house's own pages, which say only that the land has been farmed since Roman times; the year is kept out of the prose.

The DOCG of 2008 is the Codex region record's, and the first in Lazio follows from it (Frascati's two DOCGs date from 2011); the DOC year of 1973 rests on two writers' sites and is left out, the story saying only that the appellation had long been a DOC.
Living names met, none in the fragment: the owner who took over in the 1980s and once led the Cesanese consortium, and his consultant agronomist, for people.json.

Left out for want of a second source: the replanting with Cesanese di Affile from 1982, the claim that the house was the first to age Cesanese in small French barriques (in 1999 by one account), and the counts of hectares.

wine.name: Mater Matuta
wine.grapes: Syrah, the great majority, with Petit Verdot for the rest.
wine.sites: The estate's vineyards at Le Ferriere, on the reclaimed plain of the Agro Pontino south of Rome, close to the remains of the temple of Mater Matuta at ancient Satricum; the vines are trained on a cordon.
wine.making: The two grapes are made apart. The Syrah ferments on its native yeasts for some eighteen to twenty days under a submerged cap, with several rounds of délestage; the Petit Verdot is punched down for its tannin. Each new wine goes into its own new barriques for about two years, and the blend then rests about a year in bottle.
wine.glass: Blackberry, bilberry and black plum over roasted coffee bean, black pepper and liquorice; full in body and silky, with ripe, dense tannin and a long, warm finish.
wine.ageing: Dense and firm when young, it opens after five years or so and keeps well beyond a decade, a long life the house credits to its Petit Verdot.
wine.serve: 16 to 18 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle an hour or two ahead; a large Bordeaux glass.

records.table: Casale del Giglio's Mater Matuta is Syrah with a little Petit Verdot from the reclaimed Agro Pontino south of Rome, named for the goddess whose temple stood beside the vineyards. Dark, silky and peppery after two years in new barriques, it wants an hour in a decanter.
records.story: The plain at Le Ferriere, south of Rome, holds the site of ancient Satricum, where digging begun in 1896 by a French archaeologist, and soon taken over by the Italian state, uncovered the temple of Mater Matuta, goddess of the dawn and of birth. The land around it was then the Pontine Marshes; their draining began in earnest in 1927, and Littoria, the new town of the Agro Pontino, was founded in 1932 and later renamed Latina. In 1967 a founder from Amatrice, in the mountains of the north of the region, set up Casale del Giglio on the reclaimed plain, in country whose fitness for the vine was largely untried. In 1977 Dutch archaeologists returned and in their first week found the Lapis Satricanus, an early Latin inscription. In 1985, with the region's leave, the house began a research project, planting fifty seven varieties in trial rows; from 1990, by the house's account, grapes such as Syrah and Petit Verdot were admitted as recommended for the province, and some twenty were kept. Mater Matuta, Syrah with Petit Verdot and named for the goddess of the temple beside its vines, became the flagship. From 2012 the house also revived Bellone from old ungrafted vines on the sands of Anzio. To a sommelier Mater Matuta shows how a young estate on new land made its name with grapes from France.

questions.q: Casale del Giglio's flagship is named for a goddess whose temple stood beside its vineyards. In which year was that temple at Satricum found?
questions.exp: Digging begun by a French archaeologist in 1896 uncovered the temple near Le Ferriere; Dutch archaeologists returned in 1977 and found the Lapis Satricanus, and the estate was founded in 1967.

The plan's note is answered: 1967 at Le Ferriere is the house's own date (its history and press pages); the blend of Syrah with Petit Verdot is the house's, about 85 and 15 per cent by Callmewine, Vino.com and other merchants; the temple's remains close to the vineyards at Le Ferriere are on the house's Mater Matuta page, the find of 1896 and the Dutch return of 1977 on the University of Amsterdam's Satricum pages and Wikipedia.

About two years in new barriques and about a year in bottle rest on merchants (22 to 24 months and 10 to 12 months on Callmewine and Italian Wine Selection, two years and at least one in bottle on another); the house's page gives first fill barriques but no length.

The founder is named Dino on the house's history page and Berardino, of Amatrice, on another of its pages; no source gave his dates, so he is described. The owner and the house's oenologist, both living, are not named and are for people.json.

The 1985 project (close to sixty varieties, fifty seven planted for study, some twenty kept), the early results of Syrah and Petit Verdot (another house page says Cabernet Sauvignon and Petit Verdot), Anthium's ungrafted vines near Anzio and Nettuno and the project of 2012 are the house's own account; the Petit Verdot note is the house's page for that wine.
The reclamation's start in earnest in 1927 is the Comune di Latina's own history; Littoria's founding in 1932 and its later name stand on the Comune, Britannica and Wikipedia.

Left out for want of a source: Mater Matuta's first vintage (the oldest seen is 2004), the French archaeologist's name and dates, and the claim that the Lapis Satricanus is the oldest Latin inscription of its kind.
